intro.html: Two tiny Latin parts open a whole family of words. bene- means well (you know it from benefit), and mal- means badly (you know it from malfunction). Put one in front of another part and you get a word for good will or for ill will.
bene- = well, good. mal- = badly, bad. A bene- word usually points to kindness or help; a mal- word points to harm, illness or trouble.
Each card has a picture and a memory hook: a sound-alike that acts out the meaning. Say the hook out loud, look at the picture, then read the sentences to see the word at work.

words.def: kind and wishing good for others
words.ex: The {benevolent} neighbor shoveled every driveway on the street after the storm.
words.ctx: Though the old shopkeeper looked stern, the town knew him to be {benevolent}; every winter he quietly paid the heating bills of families who could not.
words.etym: From Latin benevolens, “wishing well”: bene (well) + volens (wishing).

mn.text: Every Saturday, Ben volunteers at the bread table; a man who gives his time to help others is {benevolent}.

scene.alt: Ben, in an apron, hands out free bread to happy children.

words.def: a person who gives money or help to a person or cause
words.ex: An unnamed {benefactor} paid for the new playground.
words.ctx: The museum could never have bought the painting on its own; a {benefactor} who loved art covered the whole cost and asked only that the public be allowed to see it.
words.etym: From Latin benefactor, “one who does good”: bene (well) + facere (to do).

mn.cue: the owner of the BENEFIT FACTORY
mn.text: Picture a factory that makes good things for other people: its owner, the {benefactor}, is the one who gives.

scene.alt: A gentleman in a top hat gives a bag of money; a woman cheers beside a sign for a new library.

words.ex: Reading aloud every evening proved {beneficial} to her spelling.
words.ctx: The new bus route proved {beneficial} to the whole neighborhood: workers reached their jobs faster, and the shops near each stop saw more customers.

roots.means: having to do with (an adjective ending)

words.etym: From Latin beneficium, “a kindness, a favor”: bene (well) + facere (to do).

mn.text: A fish that sweeps the sea floor clean helps every creature around it; its work is {beneficial}.

scene.alt: A smiling fish sweeps the sea floor clean with a broom.

words.def: gentle and kind; also, not harmful
words.ex: Despite his size, the farm’s old horse was {benign} and let the children brush his mane.
words.ctx: The rumor about the new rule sounded alarming, but the change turned out to be {benign}: it did nothing except change the color of the hall passes.
words.etym: From Latin benignus, “kindly, good-natured,” from bene (well).
words.note: Doctors use benign for a growth that is not harmful; the opposite is malignant.

mn.cue: BE NINE: a big dog named Nine
mn.text: The family dog, Nine, is huge, but he is {benign}: he lets the kitten nap on his back.

scene.alt: A huge dog named Nine stands calmly while a kitten naps on his back.

words.def: a person who receives a benefit, such as money left in a will
words.ex: Lila was the {beneficiary} of her grandfather’s garden and all his tools.
words.ctx: When the old sailor died, his will named the town library as the {beneficiary} of his whole collection of maps, so anyone can now come and study them.
words.etym: From Latin beneficiarius, “one who receives a favor,” from beneficium, a kindness.

mn.cue: the one who gets the FISH
mn.text: The fisherman gives; the boy who gets the fish is the bene-FISH-iary. The {beneficiary} is the one who receives.

scene.alt: A fisherman gives a fish to a delighted boy; the giver is labeled gives, the boy gets.

words.ex: In the old story, a {malevolent} sorcerer cast a spell of endless winter on the valley.
words.ctx: The villain’s grin was not friendly but {malevolent}; he was already planning how to ruin the festival for everyone in town.
words.etym: From Latin malevolens, “wishing ill”: male (badly) + volens (wishing).

mn.text: An evil villain sneaks through the mall wishing bad luck on every shopper: he is {malevolent}.

cast.think: I wish them all bad luck!

scene.alt: A caped villain sneaks through a store, wishing everyone bad luck; a girl looks worried.

words.def: meaning to hurt someone on purpose
words.ex: Spreading a {malicious} rumor can hurt a person’s friendships for years.
words.ctx: The broken window was no accident; the footprints and the thrown rock showed that the damage was {malicious}.
words.etym: From Latin malitia, “badness, ill will,” from malus (bad).

mn.text: Sneaky Mal pours salt into the baker’s delicious pie on purpose; spoiling it just to hurt her is {malicious}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man pours salt into a pie while the baker is not looking.

words.def: an illness, or a deep-rooted problem
words.ex: Boredom is a common {malady} on long car trips.
words.ctx: The town’s real {malady} was not its empty storefronts but its loss of hope; once neighbors began working together, the shops slowly filled again.
words.etym: From Old French maladie, from malade, “sick,” from Latin male habitus, “in poor condition.”

mn.text: Poor Granny Mae is the lady with the bad cold; her {malady} keeps her in bed.

scene.alt: An old lady lies in bed with a bad cold, sneezing.

words.def: to say harmful and untrue things about someone
words.ex: It is unfair to {malign} a teammate who is not there to answer.
words.ctx: Rather than bake better bread, the rival shop tried to {malign} its new neighbor, telling customers false stories about its kitchen.
words.etym: From Latin malignus, “ill-natured,” the opposite of benignus.
words.note: Malign is also an adjective meaning evil or harmful (a malign influence), but it is most often a verb.

mn.text: A mean line about someone that is not true: whispering “Dev cheats!” is a way to {malign} him.

labels.text: MAL LINE = a lie that hurts

scene.alt: A sneaky teen whispers a false rumor about Dev, who looks hurt.

words.def: a person who is always dissatisfied and complaining
words.ex: Even on a perfect beach day, the {malcontent} found something to grumble about.
words.ctx: Most of the crew liked the new schedule, but one {malcontent} complained about it at every meeting and refused even to try it.
words.etym: From French malcontent, “ill content”: mal (badly) + content (satisfied).

mn.text: Grandpa Gus is never content, not even at the beach: he is a {malcontent}.

scene.alt: A grumpy grandfather complains on a lovely beach while his wife enjoys the sun.

after.cap: Pairs that share a second part: bene- and mal- flip the meaning.

after.html: Keep the giver and the receiver straight: a benefactor gives and a beneficiary receives. The ending -or names the one who does something, as in actor and donor.

items.q: The museum thanked the ______ who paid for its new wing. Which word fits?
items.why: The person who paid gave the help, so that person is the benefactor: the giver.

items.q: Grandma left her piano to Lila in her will. Lila is the piano’s…
items.why: Lila receives the gift, so she is the beneficiary: the receiver.

items.q: Which word does NOT contain the Latin part mal- (badly)?
items.why: A mall, a shopping center, only begins with the same letters; it comes from the name of an old game played with a mallet, not from mal-.

items.q: True or false: malign can be a verb meaning to say harmful, untrue things about someone.
items.why: True. To malign someone is to speak ill of them falsely.
